sysd-q-003.title: Instant messaging
sysd-q-003.text: Email conversations are not real time. Instant messaging is. It is synchronous communication that sends messages in real time between two or more parties over the Internet or another computer network. A reply can arrive at once. It covers private messaging between two users and chat rooms or groups. Modern apps go beyond text to multimedia, emojis, file transfer, voice calling and video chat, and they connect known users through a contact list or chat rooms. Most services run as centralized networks on the operator's servers, unlike peer-to-peer protocols such as XMPP. Most protocols are proprietary, so users cannot reach people on other networks. Storing messages in the cloud carries a risk that the provider holds the decryption keys and can read them. Encryption is the main way apps protect privacy, and {{ref:sysd-q-070}} can be on by default.

sysd-q-070.title: End-to-end encryption
sysd-q-070.text: Encrypting a chat does not help much if the company running it can still read the chat. End-to-end encryption closes that gap. It is a way of building a secure communication system in which only the sender and the intended recipients can read the messages. The sender's device encrypts each message so that no third party, including the provider, can decrypt it, and recipients decrypt it on their own devices. Encryption in transit alone is not enough, because providers can read messages that pass through their intermediaries and storage. Server-side disk encryption is not enough either, since the provider holds the keys. Around 2014, when WhatsApp encrypted part of its network, the term came to require that neither the provider nor an attacker in transit can decrypt. The protection stops at the endpoints, though. A hacked device can leak the key or the decrypted messages, and a backdoor, a secret way of bypassing normal encryption, can undo the design.

sysd-q-069.title: Store and forward
sysd-q-069.text: A text sent through {{ref:sysd-q-076}} to a phone that cannot be reached does not vanish. It waits at a service center until the phone is reachable again. That is store and forward. Data goes to an intermediate station that keeps it in storage and sends it on later, to its destination or to another intermediate station. The station verifies the integrity of the message before forwarding it. A switching center accepts a message from the sender, holds it, and forwards it according to the priority the sender set and the availability of an outgoing channel. If the destination is unreachable, the center keeps the message and retries later, which raises the chance of delivery. If the destination is available, the message goes at once. Email over SMTP works the same way. The technique suits networks with intermittent connectivity, high mobility, long delays, high error rates or no direct end-to-end connection. Its limit is speed: delay-tolerant store-and-forward networks offer no real-time services.

sysd-q-072.title: Signal Protocol
sysd-q-072.text: WhatsApp built the Signal Protocol into its clients after a November 2014 partnership, and by April 2016 every form of communication on WhatsApp was end-to-end encrypted. The protocol is a non-federated cryptographic protocol, formerly called the TextSecure Protocol, that provides {{ref:sysd-q-070}} for voice and instant messaging conversations. It combines the Double Ratchet Algorithm, prekeys and a key agreement protocol. Prekeys are one-time ephemeral public keys uploaded in advance to a central server. The ratchet pairs an ephemeral key exchange with a symmetric-key ratchet, and it added offline messages and better resilience to out-of-order messages. It is called self-healing because after an attacker compromises a session key it automatically blocks access to the cleartext of later messages. The protocol gives confidentiality, integrity, authentication, forward secrecy and post-compromise security, but not anonymity, and it needs servers to relay messages and store public key material. Group chats combine a pairwise double ratchet with multicast encryption. Users can compare public key fingerprints through an outside channel to avoid a man-in-the-middle attack.

sysd-q-071.title: End-to-end encryption versus provider access
sysd-q-071.text: Should the company that runs a chat service be able to read your messages? Without end-to-end encryption, a provider can easily offer search and scan for illegal content. But anyone with access to the stored data, by design or through a backdoor, can read it too. With the encryption, the provider cannot hand over decrypted messages on government request. Governments, law enforcement agencies and child protection groups worry about criminal investigations. Security experts and privacy advocates defend the encryption. Some governments have passed laws targeting it, while the UK's Information Commissioner's Office and the US's CISA argue for its use.

sysd-q-073.title: Messaging metadata and sealed sender
sysd-q-073.text: Encrypt every word of a message and a server can still see who talks to whom, and when. The Signal Protocol does not stop a provider from keeping that metadata. Signal says it keeps recipient identifiers only as long as needed to send each message. The closest thing to metadata it stores is each user's last connection time, with precision reduced to the day. Sealed sender hides the sender from the server: the sender's identity travels inside each message, encrypted with a key the server lacks. A simultaneous wiretap of the device or servers can still show that its IP address contacted a server at certain times.

sysd-q-004.title: Chat application on Redis pub/sub
sysd-q-004.text: Redis can play two roles in a simple chat app: it stores the messages and it announces them. The server publishes each chat message to a topic that subscribers pick up. A web socket connects client and server. The pub-sub server opens several connections to Redis: one updates the data models and publishes, the others subscribe and listen. On connecting, the client gets the member list and history from Redis. A new member is announced on the member_add topic. A new message goes into a Redis sorted set with zadd, ordered by arrival time. It is published to the messages topic, so the recipient's client receives it.

sysd-q-002.title: Designing a chat service like WhatsApp
sysd-q-002.text:
A chat service like WhatsApp has to support one-on-one chat, group chats of at most 100 people and file sharing. It must be highly available with minimal latency. The extended requirements are sent, delivered and read receipts, last seen time and push notifications. Start with scale. Assume 50 million daily active users, each sending at least 10 messages to 4 different people a day. That is 2 billion messages a day, or 24K requests per second, and 5 percent of the messages are media files. At 100 bytes per message, text needs about 200 GB a day. The 100 KB media files need 10 TB a day, about 38 PB over 10 years. The 10.2 TB of daily ingress works out to around 120 MB per second.

The data model is small. Tables hold users (name, phoneNumber), messages (type, content, timestamps and a chat or group ID), chats and groups, plus two many-to-many tables, users_chats and users_groups. Each service owns its tables, in PostgreSQL or a distributed NoSQL store like Cassandra. The API has four calls. Get all chats or groups takes a user ID. Get messages takes a user ID and channel ID. Send message takes a user ID, channel ID and message, and returns a boolean result. Join or leave a channel completes the set. The system is built from microservices, which scale horizontally and decouple. Five services do the work: user (HTTP and authentication), chat, notification, presence for last seen, and media for uploads. Each owns its data, and they talk over REST or the lighter gRPC.

How does a message reach the other phone? Pulling by periodic HTTP requests or long polling does not scale, since most responses are empty. Push over WebSockets delivers data without delay and is full-duplex, unlike one-way Server-Sent Events, and a cache of active connections shows who is online. The sender's chat service has the sequencing service give the message a unique ID, persists it and queues it for sync. If the recipient is online, the message is pushed over their web socket. Otherwise it goes via the push server. The chat service queues an event with device-platform metadata, and the notification service forwards it to {{ref:sysd-q-074}} or {{ref:sysd-q-075}}. The queues give best-effort ordering and at-least-once delivery.

Receipts and last seen ride on the same connection. On login the client opens a web socket, and the presence service updates the user's status and notifies friends. For last seen, the client sends a heartbeat ping and the last active timestamp is kept in a Redis or Memcached cache. A client acknowledgment (ACK) shows a message was delivered and sets its deliveredAt field. The message is marked seen, setting seenAt, once the user opens the chat.

Storage grows fastest in media. Partition the database horizontally by hash, list, range or composite schemes, with consistent hashing against uneven load, as in {{ref:sysd-scale-087}}. Cache older messages with LRU eviction, and paginate group history so users with limited bandwidth load old messages only on request. The media service keeps files in object storage such as Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage or Google Cloud Storage, or in HDFS or GlusterFS. Static files are served from a CDN such as CloudFront or Cloudflare. Multimedia is sent by uploading the image, audio or video to an HTTP server, then sending a link to the content with its Base64 encoded thumbnail where applicable.

To remove single points of failure, run multiple service instances, load balancers, read replicas and a replicated cache. Keep a standby API Gateway too, the one entry point for HTTP, WebSocket and TCP/IP. Kafka or NATS make notifications robust. WhatsApp itself uses {{ref:sysd-q-069}}. Its server stores a message, tries to forward it to the addressee and repeatedly requests acknowledgement of receipt. It deletes the message once acknowledged or, if undelivered, after 30 days. The thing to remember: when the recipient is online the message is pushed, and when not it waits in a queue until it can be delivered.

sysd-q-005.title: How WhatsApp delivers messages
sysd-q-005.text:
In April 2012 WhatsApp handled two billion messages a day. By August of that year it was ten billion. The protocol under that traffic is a customized version of the open standard XMPP, the Extensible messaging and presence protocol. A 2019 US Department of Justice document calls it FunXMPP. An account uses the phone number as its username. The app compares the numbers in the address book with the central database of users and adds contacts to the contact list automatically.

Delivery is store and forward. A message is stored on a server, which tries to forward it and repeatedly requests acknowledgement. Once acknowledged it is deleted, and if it is still undelivered after 30 days it is deleted too. A multimedia message is uploaded to an HTTP server, and only a link to the content, plus a Base64 encoded thumbnail where applicable, travels in the message.

Messages are encrypted with the Signal Protocol, and end-to-end encryption was completed for every form of communication in April 2016. Users can verify each other's keys, and calls use SRTP. A user can link up to four devices to one account. They sync with the primary phone, which originally had to stay online for them to work, until multi-device support removed that requirement.

sysd-q-093.title: Apache Lucene
sysd-q-093.text: Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, CrateDB, MongoDB Atlas Search and Netflix's search all rest on the same core, Apache Lucene. Lucene is a free and open-source search engine software library, originally written in Java, and a widely used foundation for production search. It suits any application that needs full-text indexing and searching. It is only a library, with no crawling or HTML parsing, so projects such as Apache Nutch extend it with both. It also offers fuzzy search based on edit distance, and its MoreLikeThis class recommends similar documents by term-vector similarity.

sysd-q-092.title: Fan-out
sysd-q-092.text: One message, many destinations. In messaging middleware, fan-out is the pattern that delivers one message to one or several destinations, possibly in parallel, without halting the sender to wait for any response. AMQP can be used with routing schemes such as point-to-point, fan-out, publish/subscribe and request-response, which version 1.0 of the standard leaves to the implementation or the network protocol. The pattern also appears inside a system. A single incoming request can trigger a long transitive chain of dependent requests to several systems, with high fan-out at various points.

sysd-q-021.title: Feed fan-out models
sysd-q-021.text:
Fanning out 60 thousand tweets delivered per second would overload a traditional relational database. Building a feed is intensive, especially for users who follow many accounts. Publishing a post to every follower's feed is heavy when the author has millions of followers. 

Push, or fan-out on write, sends a new tweet to all followers' feeds immediately. The system need not scan a user's followers list for updates, but database writes increase. In the primer's design a push places the tweet in each follower's home timeline in a memory cache, an O(n) operation: 1,000 followers mean 1,000 lookups and inserts. So the feed store needs fast writes, such as a NoSQL database or memory cache.

Pull, or fan-out on load, builds the feed and holds it in memory only when a follower reloads it. That cuts writes, but recent tweets appear only on request and server reads increase.

The hybrid combines both: users with fewer followers use push, while users with many followers, such as celebrities, use pull. Fan-out for users with millions of followers can take several minutes. So the primer suggests not fanning them out, and merging their tweets from search into the home timeline at serve time.

sysd-q-022.title: Feed ranking
sysd-q-022.text: Facebook's early feed ranking multiplied three numbers, while modern models weigh thousands of factors. Feed ranking scores each item in a feed by how relevant it is to a specific user, so the most relevant appear first. It can use parameters such as relevance, time and engagement. {{ref:sysd-q-091}} scored each item as Affinity × Weight × Decay. Affinity is the closeness of the user to the creator, higher when the user often likes, comments on or messages them. Weight is a value per kind of interaction, so a comment can count more than a like. Decay lowers the rank of older interactions.

sysd-q-091.title: EdgeRank
sysd-q-091.text: By 2013 the algorithm that replaced EdgeRank weighed more than 100,000 factors. EdgeRank is the name commonly given to the algorithm Facebook used to decide which posts to show in a user's News Feed. The simplified 2010 version scored posts on three parts: user affinity, content weight and a time-based decay parameter. Newer posts tend to hold a higher place than older ones. As of 2011 Facebook stopped using EdgeRank and moved to a machine learning algorithm. Such ranking shapes what users see out of what they follow, and it can produce a filter bubble when updates confirm their opinions.

sysd-q-026.title: Trending topics
sysd-q-026.text: Trending topics look like a feature of their own, but the functionality is built on top of search. It shows the queries, hashtags and topics searched most often in a recent window. The system caches the most frequently searched queries, hashtags and topics from the last N seconds. A batch job refreshes them every M seconds. The ranking algorithm can also weight trending topics and personalize them for the user.

sysd-q-020.title: Designing a social feed like Twitter
sysd-q-020.text:
A social feed like Twitter lets users post tweets of text, image or video and follow other users. They read a newsfeed of tweets from the people they follow, and they search tweets. The service must be highly available with minimal latency, and it must scale. The extended requirements are metrics and analytics, retweets and favorites. The system design primer scopes out the Twitter Firehose, filtering by visibility settings, hiding @replies to people the user does not follow, and the hide-retweets setting.

Two sets of assumptions size it. One author, Singh, assumes a read-heavy system with 1 billion total users, 200 million daily active users and 5 tweets per user per day. That gives 1 billion tweets a day and about 12K requests per second. At 100 bytes per message, text is about 100 GB a day. Media is in 10 percent of tweets at 50 KB each. That adds 5 TB a day, about 19 PB over 10 years, and about 60 MB per second of bandwidth. The primer instead assumes 100 million active users and 500 million tweets per day. It assumes an average fanout of 10 deliveries per tweet, 60 thousand tweets delivered on fanout per second and 100 thousand read requests per second.

The tables hold users, tweets (type, content, userID), favorites, followers (an N:M relation), feeds and feeds_tweets. Each service owns its tables, on PostgreSQL or a distributed NoSQL store such as Cassandra. Posting a tweet takes a user ID, content and an optional media URL. Following or unfollowing takes a follower ID and a followee ID. Getting the newsfeed takes a user ID and returns the tweets to show. A microservices architecture scales horizontally. Each service owns its data: user, newsfeed, tweet, search, media, notification and analytics. They talk over REST or the lighter gRPC, with service discovery.

The heart of the design is the feed. Building one retrieves the accounts a user follows, fetches their tweets, ranks them by relevance, time and engagement, and returns pages. Because that is intensive, feeds are pre-generated in the cache and refreshed periodically. The choice is among the models of {{ref:sysd-q-021}}. Pull builds the feed when a follower reloads, with fewer writes and more reads. Push writes each tweet into followers' feeds at once, with more writes. The hybrid pushes for users with fewer followers and pulls for celebrities. In the primer's design, posting stores the tweet in the author's SQL timeline. The fan-out service finds the followers, inserts the tweet into each home timeline in a memory cache (1,000 followers mean 1,000 inserts) and queues notifications. To read the home timeline, the timeline service gets tweet ids and user ids from the memory cache in O(1). It then fetches tweet details and user details in bulk from the tweet info and user info services in O(n).

Search uses Elasticsearch, built on {{ref:sysd-q-093}}. The search service tokenizes the query, normalizes capitalization and converts it to boolean operations. It then scatter-gathers across the cluster, asking every node and merging the answers, and ranks and sorts the results.

The fan-out service is the bottleneck. Fan-out for users with millions of followers can take several minutes, racing with @replies. So re-order at serve time, skip fanning out highly followed users, and merge their tweets in at read time. Keep only several hundred tweets per home timeline and only active users in the cache, rebuilding from SQL after 30 inactive days. Read replicas cannot absorb cache misses, so add federation, denormalization, SQL tuning and NoSQL. Cache the top 20% of tweets with LRU eviction, and paginate. Keep media in object storage behind a CDN. For resilience, run multiple service instances, load balancers and read replicas. The thing to remember: fan-out is the heart of a feed, and celebrities break the simple version of it.

sysd-q-024.title: Twitter's technology stack
sysd-q-024.text: Twitter's stack can be read layer by layer, from the phone in a user's hand down to the database. On the client side, the mobile apps use Swift and Kotlin, with a PWA, a progressive web app built to behave like an installed app. The web client uses JavaScript, React and Redux. Behind the clients, the services run on Mesos with Finagle. Below the services sit the stores. Caching, the layer that keeps frequently used data close at hand so it need not be fetched again, uses Pelikan Cache and Redis. The databases, which keep the data itself, are Manhattan, MySQL and PostgreSQL. That makes four layers: client, services, cache and database. The feed design in {{ref:sysd-q-020}} relies on the last two working together.

sysd-q-023.title: Twitter's tweet recommendation pipeline
sysd-q-023.text: A day's tweets are far too many to rank one by one. Twitter's recommendation pipeline narrows 500 million tweets to a ranked, filtered and mixed set in five stages: candidate sourcing, global filtering, scoring and ranking, filtering, and mixing. Candidate sourcing starts with the 500 million tweets, and global filtering cuts them down to 1500 candidates. Scoring and ranking then works on those candidates with a neural network of 48M parameters. A further filtering stage achieves author and content diversity, so the timeline does not rest on one author or one kind of content. The final mixing stage blends the tweets with ads recommendations and Who to Follow. The shape is a funnel: the big cut comes first, and the relevance scoring that {{ref:sysd-q-022}} describes comes after it.

openers.design-a-chat-service-like-whatsapp: A chat message looks simple: you type, someone else reads. Underneath, the service must deliver it in real time, hold it when the recipient cannot be reached, and keep it private from everyone except the two ends. This chapter starts with instant messaging itself, then covers store and forward, end-to-end encryption and the Signal Protocol, and the argument over who should be able to read messages. It ends with two designs: a worked answer to the WhatsApp interview question, and a look at how WhatsApp itself delivers messages.
openers.design-a-social-feed-like-twitter: A social feed has one job: out of everything posted, show each reader the posts worth reading, and show them fast. That takes two decisions. The first is how a new post reaches its followers' feeds, by push, by pull or by a mix of both, and the second is how the posts in a feed are scored so the most relevant appear first. The chapter begins with two building blocks, the Apache Lucene search library and the fan-out pattern, then covers feed models, ranking, EdgeRank and trending topics. It closes with the worked Twitter design, Twitter's technology stack and a pipeline that narrows 500 million tweets to a ranked, filtered and mixed set.

reviews.design-a-chat-service-like-whatsapp: Every design in this chapter bends around one promise: a message sent is a message delivered, and read by no one but the recipient. Store and forward keeps the delivery half, holding a message on a server until the phone can take it, and WhatsApp deletes it once acknowledged or after 30 days. End-to-end encryption, which WhatsApp builds on the Signal Protocol, keeps the privacy half, while metadata and the argument over provider access show where the promise stops. The worked example joins both to WebSockets, queues, presence and push notifications, and the case study shows the scale WhatsApp reached: ten billion messages a day by August 2012.
reviews.design-a-social-feed-like-twitter: A feed is built twice: once when tweets are delivered and again when they are ordered. Fan-out decides delivery, with push, pull or a hybrid for celebrities, and the 60 thousand tweets delivered per second in the primer's design are why a fast-write store is needed. Ranking decides order, from EdgeRank's three parts to models that take more than 100,000 factors into account, and Twitter's pipeline cuts 500 million tweets to 1500 before it scores them. Search built on Lucene and trending topics served from a refreshed cache sit beside the feed, and the stack case study names the tools underneath.
